title: Celsus says turning the other cheek came from Plato
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα δὲ ἴδωμεν καὶ τὴν ἑξῆς αὐτοῦ λέξιν οὕτως ἔχουσαν· ἔστιν αὐτοῖς καὶ τοιόνδε παράγγελμα, τὸν ὑβρίζοντα μὴ ἀμύνεσθαι· κἂν τύπτῃ, φησὶ, τὴν ἑτέραν γνάθον, σὺ δὲ καὶ τὴν ἄλλην πάρεχε. ἀρχαῖον καὶ τοῦτο, εὖ μάλα πρόσθεν εἰρημένον, ἀγροικότερον δ᾿ αὐτὸ ἀπεμνημόνευσαν. ἐπεὶ καὶ Πλάτωνι πεποίηται Σωκράτης Κρίτωνι διαλεγόμενος τάδε· „οὐδαμῶς ἄρα δεῖ ἀδικεῖν. οὐ δῆτα. οὐδ᾿ ἀδικούμενον ἄρα ἀνταδικεῖν, ὡς οἱ πολλοὶ οἴονται. ἐπειδή γε οὐδαμῶς δεῖ ἀδικεῖν. οὐ φαίνεται. τί δὲ δή; κακουργεῖν δεῖ, ὦ Κρίντων. ἢ οὔ; οὐ δεῖ δή που, ὦ Σώκρατες. τί δέ; ἀντικακουργεῖν καὶ κακῶς πάσχοντα, ὡς οἱ πολλοί φασι, δίκαιον ἢ οὐ δίκαιον; οὐδαμῶς. τὸ γάρ που κακῶς ποιεῖν ἀνθρώπους τοῦ ἀδικεῖν οὐδὲν διαφέρει. ἀληθῆ λέγεις. οὔτε ἄρα ἀνταδικεῖν δεῖ οὐδὲ κακῶς ποιεῖν οὐδένα ἀνθρώπων, οὐδα᾿ ἂν ὁτιοῦν πάσχῃ παρ᾿ αὐτῶν.“ ταῦτά φησιν ὁ Πλάτων καὶ αὖθις τάδε· „σκόπει οὖν δὴ καὶ σὺ εὖ μάλα. πότερον κοινωνεῖς καὶ συνδοκεῖ σοι, καὶ ἀρχώμεθα ἐντεῦθεν βουλευόμενοι, ὡς οὐδέποτε ὀρθῶς ἔχοντος οὔτε τοῦ ἀδικεῖν οὔτε τοῦ ἀνταδικεῖν οὔτε κακῶς πάσχοντα ἀμύνεσθαι ἀντιδρῶντα κακῶς· ἢ ἀφίστασαι καὶ οὐ κοινωνεῖς τῆς ἀρχῆς; ἐμοὶ μὲν γὰρ καὶ πάλαι οὕτως καὶ νῦν ἔτι δοκεῖ.“ Πλάτωνι μὲν οὖν οὕτως ἤρεσεν, ἦν δὲ καὶ πρόσθεν ἔτι θείοις ἀνδράσι δεδογμένα. ἀλλὰ τῶνδε μὲν πέρι καὶ τῶν ἄλλων. ὅσα παραφθείρουσιν, ἀρκείτω τὰ εἰρημένα· καὶ ὅτῳ φίλον ἐπὶ πλεῖόν τι αὐτῶν ζητεῖν, εἴσεται.
pass_a_gloss: After these, let us see (εἶδον) also his next text (λέξις), running thus: [Celsus:] There is for them also such a precept (παράγγελμα): not to retaliate against (ἀμύνομαι) the one insulting (ὑβρίζω); 'and if he strikes (τύπτω),' he says, 'the one jaw (γνάθος), you offer (παρέχω) also the other.' Ancient (ἀρχαῖος) this too, very well said before, but more rustically (ἀγροικότερον) they recorded (ἀπομνημονεύω) it. Since also by Plato Socrates is made, conversing with Crito, [to say] these: 'In no way then must one do wrong (ἀδικέω). – Not indeed. – Nor then, being wronged, to wrong in return (ἀνταδικέω), as the many think, since in no way must one do wrong. – It appears not. – What then? Must one do evil (κακουργέω), Crito, or not? – One must not, surely, Socrates. – What? To do evil in return (ἀντικακουργέω) when suffering evil, as the many say, just or not just? – Not at all. For doing evil to men differs in nothing from doing wrong. – You say true. – Then one must neither wrong in return nor do evil to any of men, not even if one suffers anything whatever from them.' These Plato says, and again these: 'Consider then you too very well whether you share (κοινωνέω) and it seems good with you (συνδοκεῖ), and let us begin deliberating (βουλεύομαι) from here, as never being right (ὀρθῶς ἔχειν) either wronging or wronging in return or, suffering evil, defending oneself (ἀμύνομαι) by doing evil in return (ἀντιδράω); or do you stand apart (ἀφίσταμαι) and not share the starting point (ἀρχή)? For to me both long ago so and now still it seems (δοκεῖ).' To Plato then thus it pleased (ἀρέσκω), but it had been decided (δοκέω, pf. pass.) even before still by divine men (θεῖοι ἄνδρες). But about these and the other things which they corrupt (παραφθείρω), let the things said suffice; and to whomever it is dear to seek (ζητέω) further into them, he will know (εἴσεται).
pass_b_english: After this, let us look also at his next passage, which runs as follows: “They also have a precept of this kind: not to retaliate against anyone who insults them. ‘And if he strikes one cheek,’ he says, ‘offer the other as well’ (Matthew 5:39; Luke 6:29). This too is ancient, and was said very well before them, but they have related it more crudely. For Plato too has Socrates say this in conversation with Crito: ‘Then one must in no way do wrong. – Certainly not. – Then neither must one who is wronged do wrong in return, as the many think, since one must in no way do wrong. – It seems not. – What then? Must one do harm, Crito, or not? – Surely one must not, Socrates. – What then? To do harm in return when one suffers harm, as the many say: is that just or not just? – Not at all. For doing harm to men surely differs in no way from doing wrong. – You speak the truth. – Then one must neither do wrong in return nor do harm to any man, whatever one may suffer at their hands’ (Plato, Crito 49b–c).

“These are Plato’s words, and again he says this: ‘Consider then, you too, very carefully, whether you share this view and agree with it, and let us begin our deliberation from this point: that it is never right either to do wrong, or to do wrong in return, or, when one suffers harm, to defend oneself by doing harm in return. Or do you stand apart and not share this starting point? For so it seemed to me long ago, and so it seems to me still’ (Plato, Crito 49d–e). This, then, was Plato’s view; but it had been held still earlier by divine men. But about these things, and all the others which they corrupt, let what has been said suffice; and whoever wishes to inquire further into any of them will find out.”

choices.choice: The whole chapter is Celsus’s text: Origen introduces it as his λέξις, and in 7.61 he quotes its last sentence back as Celsus’s words; so it stands in double quotation marks, with the Gospel saying and Plato in single marks inside. Celsus’s form of the saying is a paraphrase: τύπτῃ and πάρεχε are closest to Luke 6:29 (τῷ τύπτοντί σε ... πάρεχε καὶ τὴν ἄλλην), while ‘one cheek ... the other’ answers Matthew 5:39; γνάθον (jaw, cheek) is his own word for the Gospels’ σιαγών. Crito 49b–c and 49d–e are quoted with small differences from the Plato manuscripts (παρ᾿ αὐτῶν for ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν; σκόπει οὖν δή); the dialogue turns between Socrates and Crito are marked with dashes, without speaker names, as in the Greek. Staged text typos read as intended: Κρίντων = Κρίτων, οὐδα᾿ = οὐδ᾿. ὑβρίζοντα: one who insults or outrages. ἀμύνεσθαι: ‘retaliate’ (defend oneself by striking back). ἀπεμνημόνευσαν: ‘related’ (literally ‘related from memory’). θείοις ἀνδράσι left as Celsus’s vague ‘divine men’. εἴσεται: ‘will find out’ (literally ‘will know’).
λέξιν: 'statement' -> 'passage' (Origen is quoting a stretch of text)
τὸν ὑβρίζοντα μὴ ἀμύνεσθαι: mixed 'oneself ... him' -> 'not to retaliate against anyone who insults them'
Gospel saying reordered into natural English: 'And if he strikes one cheek,' he says, 'offer the other as well'
τῶν ἄλλων ὅσα: 'the others which' -> 'all the others which'
opening quotation mark added at the start of the second paragraph, since Celsus's quotation continues
Crito 49b–c and 49d–e checked: wording and order match; all dialogue turns kept
